title: Native event history does not prove consumer intent or progress
applies_when: An asynchronous stream handoff or lifecycle repair infers current caller intent from past events, or a regression only checks state flags without exercising normal consumption.
lesson: Use the actual runtime and owner entry to check explicit operation sequences and observable consumer progress. In Node readable streams, pause() need not emit a new pause event when already non-flowing, and removing a readable listener can schedule an automatic resume for data consumers. A historical resume event therefore cannot represent the latest caller intent. Keep pause-only, resume-then-pause, normal flowing consumption and async iteration as distinct controls; verify buffered bytes and EOF as well as state. A repair can preserve a pause flag yet stall normal consumers.
avoid_when: These Node transition mechanisms are not universal to other stream libraries or runtime versions. A portable helper/owner-entry probe is not POSIX IPC transfer, whole-application, performance or PR qualification. Do not remove buffering guards or suppress native exit draining solely from a narrow state test.

evidence.note: pause() emits only on a flowing-state transition; updateReadableListening may resume when data listeners remain. This pinned native implementation explains the mechanism, not a general repair guarantee.
The official reading-mode contract distinguishes flowing data consumption, readable-event consumption and asynchronous iteration. Test the intended consumer API, not a guessed common mode.

The handoff holds reads, installs a readable listener and later uses recorded resume intent. This is a source example to inspect alongside the actual caller and native runtime; it does not qualify any proposed fix.
